questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A monochromatic source of light operating at 15 kW emits $2.5 \times 10^{22}$ photons $/s$ . The region of an electromagnetic spectrum to which the emitted electromagnetic radiation belongs to $____$ 。 (Take $ℎ=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J.s$ and $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ ).
questions.question_html:
A monochromatic source of light operating at 15 kW emits $2.5 \times 10^{22}$ photons $/s$ . The region of an electromagnetic spectrum to which the emitted electromagnetic radiation belongs to $____$ 。

(Take $ℎ=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J.s$ and $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ ).
questions.explanation_text: The power $(P)$ of a light source is the total energy emitted per unit time. If the source emits n photons per second, and each photon has an energy E , then the power is: $P=n \times E$ The given power of the source is $P=15kW=15 \times 10^{3}W$ and the number of photons per second is $n=2.5 \times 10^{22}s^{-1}$ $E=\frac{P}{n}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=\frac{15 \times 10^{3}}{2.5 \times 10^{22}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=6 \times 10^{-19}J$ The energy of a photon is related to its wavelength by the formula: $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda} \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{ℎc}{E}$ Substituting the constants and energy, The Plank's constant is $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J \cdot s$ , The speed of light is $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ $\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{6 \times 10^{-19}}m$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{19.8 \times 10^{-26}}{6 \times 10^{-19}}m$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=3.3 \times 10^{-7}m$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=3.3 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{9}nm=330nm$ Visible light typically ranges from approximately 400 nm to 700 nm . And the ultraviolet (UV) radiation ranges from approximately 10 nm to 400 nm . Since 330 nm is less than 400 nm , the radiation belongs to the ultraviolet region. Therefore, the emitted radiation belongs to the Ultraviolet region. Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
The power $(P)$ of a light source is the total energy emitted per unit time. If the source emits n photons per second, and each photon has an energy E , then the power is:

$P=n \times E$

The given power of the source is $P=15kW=15 \times 10^{3}W$ and the number of photons per second is $n=2.5 \times 10^{22}s^{-1}$

$E=\frac{P}{n}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=\frac{15 \times 10^{3}}{2.5 \times 10^{22}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=6 \times 10^{-19}J$

The energy of a photon is related to its wavelength by the formula:

$E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda} \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{ℎc}{E}$

Substituting the constants and energy,

The Plank's constant is $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J \cdot s$ ,

The speed of light is $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$

$\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{6 \times 10^{-19}}m$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{19.8 \times 10^{-26}}{6 \times 10^{-19}}m$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=3.3 \times 10^{-7}m$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=3.3 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{9}nm=330nm$

Visible light typically ranges from approximately 400 nm to 700 nm . And the ultraviolet (UV) radiation ranges from approximately 10 nm to 400 nm . Since 330 nm is less than 400 nm , the radiation belongs to the ultraviolet region.

Therefore, the emitted radiation belongs to the Ultraviolet region.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: Light source having wavelength 331 nm is used to generate photo-electrons whose stopping potential is 0.2 V . The work function of the used metal in the experiment is $\alpha \times 10^{-19}J$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ . $(h=6.62 \times 10^{-34}Js,e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C\text{and}c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s)$
questions.question_html:
Light source having wavelength 331 nm is used to generate photo-electrons whose stopping potential is 0.2 V . The work function of the used metal in the experiment is $\alpha \times 10^{-19}J$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .

$(h=6.62 \times 10^{-34}Js,e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C\text{and}c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s)$
questions.explanation_text: If the energy of an incident photon is $E$ then it is equal to the energy required to overcome the work function $(\phi)$ of the metal and the maximum kinetic energy ( $K_{max}$ ) to the emitted electron. $E=\phi+K_{max}$ Therefore, $\phi=E-K_{max}$ . Energy is given by $E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$ where the Planck's constant $h=6.62 \times 10^{-34}Js$ , the speed of light $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ , and the wavelength of light is $\lambda=331nm=331 \times 10^{-9}m$ : Putting the values, $E=\frac{(6.62 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3 \times 10^{8})}{331 \times 10^{-9}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=\frac{19.86 \times 10^{-26}}{331 \times 10^{-9}}=\frac{1986 \times 10^{-28}}{331 \times 10^{-9}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=6 \times 10^{-19}J$ The maximum kinetic energy is related to the stopping potential ( $V_{0}$ ) by: $K_{max}=eV_{0}$ The electronic charge is $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C$ and the stopping potential is $V_{0}=0.2V$ : $K_{max}=(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \times 0.2=0.32 \times 10^{-19}J$ So, the work function of metal is, $\phi=E-K_{max}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\phi=(6 \times 10^{-19})-(0.32 \times 10^{-19})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\phi=5.68 \times 10^{-19}J=\alpha \times 10^{-19}J \Rightarrow \alpha=5.68$ Therefore, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
If the energy of an incident photon is $E$ then it is equal to the energy required to overcome the work function $(\phi)$ of the metal and the maximum kinetic energy ( $K_{max}$ ) to the emitted electron.

$E=\phi+K_{max}$

Therefore, $\phi=E-K_{max}$ .

Energy is given by $E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$ where the Planck's constant $h=6.62 \times 10^{-34}Js$ , the speed of light $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ , and the wavelength of light is $\lambda=331nm=331 \times 10^{-9}m$ :

Putting the values,

$E=\frac{(6.62 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3 \times 10^{8})}{331 \times 10^{-9}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=\frac{19.86 \times 10^{-26}}{331 \times 10^{-9}}=\frac{1986 \times 10^{-28}}{331 \times 10^{-9}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=6 \times 10^{-19}J$

The maximum kinetic energy is related to the stopping potential ( $V_{0}$ ) by:

$K_{max}=eV_{0}$

The electronic charge is $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C$ and the stopping potential is $V_{0}=0.2V$ :

$K_{max}=(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \times 0.2=0.32 \times 10^{-19}J$

So, the work function of metal is,

$\phi=E-K_{max}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\phi=(6 \times 10^{-19})-(0.32 \times 10^{-19})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\phi=5.68 \times 10^{-19}J=\alpha \times 10^{-19}J \Rightarrow \alpha=5.68$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: Number of photons of equal energy emitted per second by a 6 mW laser source operating at 663 nm is ________. (Given : $ℎ=6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J.s and $c=3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s)
questions.question_html:
Number of photons of equal energy emitted per second by a 6 mW laser source operating at 663 nm is ________.
(Given : $ℎ=6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J.s and $c=3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s)
questions.explanation_text: The power $(P)$ of the laser source is, $P=6mW=6 \times 10^{-3}J/s$ The wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of the emitted photon is $\lambda=663nm=663 \times 10^{-9}m$ Planck's constant $h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}J \cdot s$ Speed of light $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$ The energy of a single photon is given by : $E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$ Total Power is the number of photons per second multiplied by the energy of one photon: $P=n \times E \Rightarrow n=\frac{P}{E}=\frac{P\lambda}{hc}$ Substituting the given values into the equation : $n=\frac{(6 \times 10^{-3}) \times (663 \times 10^{-9})}{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3 \times 10^{8})}$ $\Rightarrow$ $n=\frac{600}{3} \times \frac{10^{-12}}{10^{-26}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $n=200 \times 10^{14}$ $\Rightarrow$ $n=2 \times 10^{16}$ Therefore, the laser source emits $2 \times 10^{16}$ photons every second. Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
The power $(P)$ of the laser source is, $P=6mW=6 \times 10^{-3}J/s$

The wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of the emitted photon is $\lambda=663nm=663 \times 10^{-9}m$

Planck's constant $h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}J \cdot s$

Speed of light $c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s$

The energy of a single photon is given by :

$E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$

Total Power is the number of photons per second multiplied by the energy of one photon:

$P=n \times E \Rightarrow n=\frac{P}{E}=\frac{P\lambda}{hc}$

Substituting the given values into the equation :

$n=\frac{(6 \times 10^{-3}) \times (663 \times 10^{-9})}{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3 \times 10^{8})}$

$\Rightarrow$ $n=\frac{600}{3} \times \frac{10^{-12}}{10^{-26}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $n=200 \times 10^{14}$

$\Rightarrow$ $n=2 \times 10^{16}$

Therefore, the laser source emits $2 \times 10^{16}$ photons every second. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A light wave described by $E=60[sin(3 \times 10^{15})t+sin(12 \times 10^{15})t]$ (in SI units) falls on a metal surface of work function 2.8 eV . The maximum kinetic energy of ejected photoelectron is (approximately) $____$ eV. $(ℎ=6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J.s. and $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C)$
questions.question_html:
A light wave described by $E=60[sin(3 \times 10^{15})t+sin(12 \times 10^{15})t]$ (in SI units) falls on a metal surface of work function 2.8 eV . The maximum kinetic energy of ejected photoelectron is (approximately)

$____$ eV. $(ℎ=6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J.s. and $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C)$
questions.explanation_text: According to Einstein's photoelectric effect, the energy of an incident photon (E) on a metal of work function $(\phi)$ then the maximum kinetic energy $(K_{max})$ to the ejected electron is, $K_{max}=E-\phi$ The energy of a photon is given by : $E=hf=\frac{h\omega}{2\pi}$ Where : h is Planck's constant. $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the light wave. The given electric field is $E=60[sin(3 \times 10^{15})t+sin(12 \times 10^{15})t]$ The given electric field equation contains two sinusoidal terms with angular frequencies are $\omega_{1}=3 \times 10^{15}rad/s$ and $\omega_{2}=12 \times 10^{15}rad/s$ Since $K_{max}$ depends on the maximum photon energy, we must use the higher angular frequency, $\omega_{max}=12 \times 10^{15}rad/s$ , because higher frequency corresponds to higher energy per photon. The energy in Joules is $E=\frac{ℎ\omega}{2\pi}$ . $E(\text{in}eV)=\frac{h \cdot \omega_{max}}{2\pi \cdot e}$ Substituting the given values : $E=\frac{(6.6 \times 10^{-34}) \times (12 \times 10^{15})}{2 \times 3.14 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E=\frac{79.2 \times 10^{-19}}{10.048 \times 10^{-19}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $E \approx 7.88eV$ So, the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electron is, $K_{max}=E-\phi$ $\Rightarrow$ $K_{max}=7.88eV-2.8eV$ $\Rightarrow$ $K_{max}=5.08eV$ $\Rightarrow$ $K_{max} \approx 5.1eV$ Therefore, the kinetic energy of electron is approximately 5.1 eV. Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
According to Einstein's photoelectric effect, the energy of an incident photon (E) on a metal of work function $(\phi)$ then the maximum kinetic energy $(K_{max})$ to the ejected electron is,

$K_{max}=E-\phi$

The energy of a photon is given by :

$E=hf=\frac{h\omega}{2\pi}$

Where :

  • h is Planck's constant.

  • $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the light wave.

The given electric field is $E=60[sin(3 \times 10^{15})t+sin(12 \times 10^{15})t]$

The given electric field equation contains two sinusoidal terms with angular frequencies are $\omega_{1}=3 \times 10^{15}rad/s$ and $\omega_{2}=12 \times 10^{15}rad/s$

Since $K_{max}$ depends on the maximum photon energy, we must use the higher angular frequency, $\omega_{max}=12 \times 10^{15}rad/s$ , because higher frequency corresponds to higher energy per photon.

The energy in Joules is $E=\frac{ℎ\omega}{2\pi}$ .

$E(\text{in}eV)=\frac{h \cdot \omega_{max}}{2\pi \cdot e}$

Substituting the given values :

$E=\frac{(6.6 \times 10^{-34}) \times (12 \times 10^{15})}{2 \times 3.14 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E=\frac{79.2 \times 10^{-19}}{10.048 \times 10^{-19}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $E \approx 7.88eV$

So, the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electron is,

$K_{max}=E-\phi$

$\Rightarrow$ $K_{max}=7.88eV-2.8eV$

$\Rightarrow$ $K_{max}=5.08eV$

$\Rightarrow$ $K_{max} \approx 5.1eV$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of electron is approximately 5.1 eV.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: The ratio of de Broglie wavelength of a deutron with kinetic energy $E$ to that of an alpha particle with kinetic energy $2E$ , is $n:1$ . The value of $n$ is $____$ . (Assume mass of proton $=$ mass of neutron) $:$
questions.question_html:
The ratio of de Broglie wavelength of a deutron with kinetic energy $E$ to that of an alpha particle with kinetic energy $2E$ , is $n:1$ . The value of $n$ is $____$ .

(Assume mass of proton $=$ mass of neutron) $:$
questions.explanation_text: The de Broglie wavelength is given by : $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$ Since kinetic energy $K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$ , we can write momentum as $p=\sqrt{2mK}$ . Therefore: $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$ Let $m_{p}$ be the mass of a proton or neutron. Deuteron (d) consists of 1 proton and 1 neutron. The mass of deuteron is $m_{d} \approx 2m_{p}$ Kinetic Energy $K_{d}=E$ Alpha particle $(\alpha)$ consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons. The mass of alpha particle is $m_{\alpha} \approx 4m_{p}$ Kinetic Energy $K_{\alpha}=2E$ The ratio of wavelengths is : $\frac{\lambda_{d}}{\lambda_{\alpha}}=\frac{\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{d}K_{d}}}}{\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{\alpha}K_{\alpha}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{d}}} \times \sqrt{\frac{K_{\alpha}}{K_{d}}}$ Substituting the values: $\frac{\lambda_{d}}{\lambda_{\alpha}}=\sqrt{\frac{4m_{p}}{2m_{p}}} \times \sqrt{\frac{2E}{E}}=2$ So, the ratio of de-Broglie wavelengths is $2:1 \Rightarrow \frac{n}{1}=\frac{2}{1} \Rightarrow n=2$ Therefore, the value of $n$ is 2 . Hence, the correct answer is 2.
questions.explanation_html:
The de Broglie wavelength is given by :

$\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$

Since kinetic energy $K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$ , we can write momentum as $p=\sqrt{2mK}$ .

Therefore:

$\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$

Let $m_{p}$ be the mass of a proton or neutron.

Deuteron (d) consists of 1 proton and 1 neutron. The mass of deuteron is $m_{d} \approx 2m_{p}$

Kinetic Energy $K_{d}=E$

Alpha particle $(\alpha)$ consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons. The mass of alpha particle is $m_{\alpha} \approx 4m_{p}$

Kinetic Energy $K_{\alpha}=2E$

The ratio of wavelengths is :

$\frac{\lambda_{d}}{\lambda_{\alpha}}=\frac{\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{d}K_{d}}}}{\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{\alpha}K_{\alpha}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{d}}} \times \sqrt{\frac{K_{\alpha}}{K_{d}}}$

Substituting the values:

$\frac{\lambda_{d}}{\lambda_{\alpha}}=\sqrt{\frac{4m_{p}}{2m_{p}}} \times \sqrt{\frac{2E}{E}}=2$

So, the ratio of de-Broglie wavelengths is $2:1 \Rightarrow \frac{n}{1}=\frac{2}{1} \Rightarrow n=2$

Therefore, the value of $n$ is 2 . Hence, the correct answer is 2.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ be the maximum kinetic energies of photoelectrons emitted from a surface of a given material for the light of wavelength $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ , respectively. If $\lambda_{1}=2\lambda_{2}$ then the work function of material is given by :
questions.question_html: $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ be the maximum kinetic energies of photoelectrons emitted from a surface of a given material for the light of wavelength $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ , respectively. If $\lambda_{1}=2\lambda_{2}$ then the work function of material is given by :
questions.explanation_text: According to the photoelectric effect, when light of a certain frequency or wavelength hits a metal surface, it provides energy to the electrons. Part of this energy is used to overcome the attractive forces of the metal (the work function, $\phi$ ), and the remaining energy becomes the maximum kinetic energy (K) of the emitted photoelectron. The energy of an incident photon is $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ . The equation is: $E=\phi+K_{max}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\phi+K_{max}$ $\Rightarrow$ $K_{max}=\frac{hc}{\lambda}-\phi$ We are given two different wavelengths and their corresponding kinetic energies: For wavelength $\lambda_{1}$ : $K_{1}=\frac{hc}{\lambda_{1}}-\phi\dots\text{(}\text{i}\text{)}$ For wavelength $\lambda_{2}$ : $K_{2}=\frac{hc}{\lambda_{2}}-\phi\dots\text{(}\text{ii}\text{)}$ It is given that $\lambda_{1}=2\lambda_{2}$ . $K_{1}=\frac{hc}{2\lambda_{2}}-\phi\dots\text{(}\text{iii}\text{)}$ From equation (ii), we can find an expression for $\frac{hc}{\lambda_{2}}$ : $\frac{hc}{\lambda_{2}}=K_{2}+\phi$ Now, substituting this into equation (iii) : $K_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(K_{2}+\phi)-\phi$ $\Rightarrow$ $2K_{1}=K_{2}+\phi-2\phi$ $\Rightarrow$ $2K_{1}=K_{2}-\phi$ $\Rightarrow$ $\phi=K_{2}-2K_{1}$ Therefore, the work function of the material is $K_{2}-2K_{1}$ . Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
According to the photoelectric effect, when light of a certain frequency or wavelength hits a metal surface, it provides energy to the electrons. Part of this energy is used to overcome the attractive forces of the metal (the work function, $\phi$ ), and the remaining energy becomes the maximum kinetic energy (K) of the emitted photoelectron. The energy of an incident photon is $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ . The equation is:

$E=\phi+K_{max}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\phi+K_{max}$

$\Rightarrow$ $K_{max}=\frac{hc}{\lambda}-\phi$

We are given two different wavelengths and their corresponding kinetic energies:

For wavelength $\lambda_{1}$ :

$K_{1}=\frac{hc}{\lambda_{1}}-\phi\dots\text{(}\text{i}\text{)}$

For wavelength $\lambda_{2}$ :

$K_{2}=\frac{hc}{\lambda_{2}}-\phi\dots\text{(}\text{ii}\text{)}$

It is given that $\lambda_{1}=2\lambda_{2}$ .

$K_{1}=\frac{hc}{2\lambda_{2}}-\phi\dots\text{(}\text{iii}\text{)}$

From equation (ii), we can find an expression for $\frac{hc}{\lambda_{2}}$ :

$\frac{hc}{\lambda_{2}}=K_{2}+\phi$

Now, substituting this into equation (iii) :

$K_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(K_{2}+\phi)-\phi$

$\Rightarrow$ $2K_{1}=K_{2}+\phi-2\phi$

$\Rightarrow$ $2K_{1}=K_{2}-\phi$

$\Rightarrow$ $\phi=K_{2}-2K_{1}$

Therefore, the work function of the material is $K_{2}-2K_{1}$ .

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: The de Broglie wavelength associated with an electron accelerated through a potential difference V is $\lambda_{e}$ and the de Broglie wavelength associated with a proton accelerated through the same potential difference is $\lambda_{p}$ . If their corresponding masses are $m_{e}$ and $m_{p}$ , respectively, then the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths $(\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}})$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html: The de Broglie wavelength associated with an electron accelerated through a potential difference V is $\lambda_{e}$ and the de Broglie wavelength associated with a proton accelerated through the same potential difference is $\lambda_{p}$ . If their corresponding masses are $m_{e}$ and $m_{p}$ , respectively, then the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths $(\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}})$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: According to de Broglie's hypothesis, the wavelength associated with a particle of momentum p is: $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$ Where h is Planck's constant. Kinetic energy is given by $K=\frac{1}{2mv^{2}}$ . In terms of linear momentum, the kinetic energy can be written as $K=\frac{m^{2}v^{2}}{2m}=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$ Thus, momentum $p=\sqrt{2mK}$ . When a particle of charge q is accelerated through a potential difference V , the work done on it becomes its kinetic energy: $K=qV$ Substituting this into the momentum equation: $p=\sqrt{2mqV}$ So, the de-Broglie's wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$ The charge on electron is $q_{e}=e$ , so the wavelength for an electron is $\lambda_{e}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{e}eV}}$ The charge on proton is $q_{p}=e$ , so the wavelength for an proton is $\lambda_{p}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{p}eV}}$ Taking the ratio $\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}}$ : $\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}}=\frac{h/\sqrt{2m_{e}eV}}{h/\sqrt{2m_{p}eV}}=\frac{\sqrt{2m_{p}eV}}{\sqrt{2m_{e}eV}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{p}}{m_{e}}}$ Therefore, the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths is $\sqrt{\frac{m_{p}}{m_{e}}}$ . Thus, the correct option is (A).
questions.explanation_html:
According to de Broglie's hypothesis, the wavelength associated with a particle of momentum p is:

$\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$

Where h is Planck's constant.

Kinetic energy is given by $K=\frac{1}{2mv^{2}}$ .

In terms of linear momentum, the kinetic energy can be written as

$K=\frac{m^{2}v^{2}}{2m}=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$

Thus, momentum $p=\sqrt{2mK}$ .

When a particle of charge q is accelerated through a potential difference V , the work done on it becomes its kinetic energy:

$K=qV$

Substituting this into the momentum equation:

$p=\sqrt{2mqV}$

So, the de-Broglie's wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$

The charge on electron is $q_{e}=e$ , so the wavelength for an electron is $\lambda_{e}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{e}eV}}$

The charge on proton is $q_{p}=e$ , so the wavelength for an proton is $\lambda_{p}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{p}eV}}$

Taking the ratio $\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}}$ :

$\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}}=\frac{h/\sqrt{2m_{e}eV}}{h/\sqrt{2m_{p}eV}}=\frac{\sqrt{2m_{p}eV}}{\sqrt{2m_{e}eV}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\lambda_{e}}{\lambda_{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{p}}{m_{e}}}$

Therefore, the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths is $\sqrt{\frac{m_{p}}{m_{e}}}$ .

Thus, the correct option is (A).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: When a light of a given wavelength falls on a metallic surface the stopping potential for photoelectrons is 3.2 V . If a second light having wavelength twice of first light is used, the stopping potential drops to 0.7 V . The wavelength of first light is $____$ m . $(h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}J.s,e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C,c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s)$
questions.question_html:
When a light of a given wavelength falls on a metallic surface the stopping potential for photoelectrons is 3.2 V . If a second light having wavelength twice of first light is used, the stopping potential drops to 0.7 V . The wavelength of first light is $____$ m .

$(h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}J.s,e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C,c=3 \times 10^{8}m/s)$
questions.explanation_text: When a light of wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) is incident on a metal of work function $\phi$ then the maximum kinetic energy of the photo-electron is given by Einstein's photoelectric equation: $K_{max}=E-\phi \Rightarrow E=\phi+K_{max}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{hc}{\lambda}=\phi+eV_{s}$ where $V_{s}$ is the stopping potential and $\phi$ is the work function of the metal. Case 1 : Wavelength is $\lambda$ , stopping potential is 3.2 V . $\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\phi+3.2e$ .....(i) Case 2 : Wavelength is $2\lambda$ , stopping potential is 0.7 V . $\frac{hc}{2\lambda}=\phi+0.7e\dots(ii)$ Subtracting equation (ii) from equation (i) : $(\frac{hc}{\lambda}-\frac{hc}{2\lambda})=(3.2e-0.7e)$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{hc}{2\lambda}=2.5e$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{hc}{5e}$ Substituting the given values : $\lambda=\frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3 \times 10^{8})}{5 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{19.89 \times 10^{-26}}{8 \times 10^{-19}}m \approx 2.5 \times 10^{-7}m$ Therefore, the initial wavelength of light used was $2.5 \times 10^{-7}m$ . Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
When a light of wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) is incident on a metal of work function $\phi$ then the maximum kinetic energy of the photo-electron is given by Einstein's photoelectric equation:

$K_{max}=E-\phi \Rightarrow E=\phi+K_{max}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{hc}{\lambda}=\phi+eV_{s}$

where $V_{s}$ is the stopping potential and $\phi$ is the work function of the metal.

Case 1 : Wavelength is $\lambda$ , stopping potential is 3.2 V .

$\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\phi+3.2e$ .....(i)

Case 2 : Wavelength is $2\lambda$ , stopping potential is 0.7 V .

$\frac{hc}{2\lambda}=\phi+0.7e\dots(ii)$

Subtracting equation (ii) from equation (i) :

$(\frac{hc}{\lambda}-\frac{hc}{2\lambda})=(3.2e-0.7e)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{hc}{2\lambda}=2.5e$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{hc}{5e}$

Substituting the given values :

$\lambda=\frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3 \times 10^{8})}{5 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{19.89 \times 10^{-26}}{8 \times 10^{-19}}m \approx 2.5 \times 10^{-7}m$

Therefore, the initial wavelength of light used was $2.5 \times 10^{-7}m$ .

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A particle having electric charge $3 \times 10^{-19}C$ and mass $6 \times 10^{-27}kg$ is accelerated by applying an electric potential of 1.21 V . Wavelength of the matter wave associated with the particle is $\alpha \times 10^{-12}m$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ . (Take Planck's constant $=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J.s$ )
questions.question_html:
A particle having electric charge $3 \times 10^{-19}C$ and mass $6 \times 10^{-27}kg$ is accelerated by applying an electric potential of 1.21 V .

Wavelength of the matter wave associated with the particle is $\alpha \times 10^{-12}m$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .

(Take Planck's constant $=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J.s$ )
questions.explanation_text: When a particle of charge $q$ is accelerated through a potential difference $V$ , the work done on the particle is converted into its kinetic energy (K): $K=qV$ Given: Charge $q=3 \times 10^{-19}C$ Potential $V=1.21V$ $K=(3 \times 10^{-19}) \times (1.21)=3.63 \times 10^{-19}J$ The momentum ( p ) of a particle of mass m is related to its kinetic energy ( K ) by: $K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m} \Rightarrow p=\sqrt{2mK}$ Substituting $K=qV$ : $p=\sqrt{2mqV}$ The de-Broglie wavelength is given by: $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$ Substituting the expression for momentum: $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$ Substituting the given values: $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J.s,m=6 \times 10^{-27}kg,q=3 \times 10^{-19}C\text{and}V=1.21V$ So, the de-Broglie wavelength associated with the particle is, $\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times (6 \times 10^{-27}) \times (3 \times 10^{-19}) \times 1.21}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{36 \times 10^{-46} \times 1.21}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{6 \times 10^{-23} \times 1.1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{6.6 \times 10^{-23}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=1 \times 10^{-11}m=\alpha \times 10^{-12}m$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=10 \times 10^{-12}=\alpha \times 10^{-12} \Rightarrow \alpha=10$ Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 10 . Hence, the correct answer is $𝟏𝟎$ .
questions.explanation_html:
When a particle of charge $q$ is accelerated through a potential difference $V$ , the work done on the particle is converted into its kinetic energy (K):

$K=qV$

Given:

  • Charge $q=3 \times 10^{-19}C$

  • Potential $V=1.21V$

$K=(3 \times 10^{-19}) \times (1.21)=3.63 \times 10^{-19}J$

The momentum ( p ) of a particle of mass m is related to its kinetic energy ( K ) by:

$K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m} \Rightarrow p=\sqrt{2mK}$

Substituting $K=qV$ :

$p=\sqrt{2mqV}$

The de-Broglie wavelength is given by:

$\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$

Substituting the expression for momentum:

$\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$

Substituting the given values:

$h=6.6 \times 10^{-34}J.s,m=6 \times 10^{-27}kg,q=3 \times 10^{-19}C\text{and}V=1.21V$

So, the de-Broglie wavelength associated with the particle is,

$\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times (6 \times 10^{-27}) \times (3 \times 10^{-19}) \times 1.21}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{36 \times 10^{-46} \times 1.21}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{6 \times 10^{-23} \times 1.1}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{6.6 \times 10^{-23}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=1 \times 10^{-11}m=\alpha \times 10^{-12}m$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=10 \times 10^{-12}=\alpha \times 10^{-12} \Rightarrow \alpha=10$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 10 .

Hence, the correct answer is $𝟏𝟎$ .

questions.question_text: An electron is travelling with a velocity $v$ in free space and when it enters a medium, its velocity is reduced by $20%$ . The de Broglie wavelength of electron in the medium is $\alpha\lambda_{0}$ , where $\lambda_{0}$ is its de Broglie wavelength in free space. The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html: An electron is travelling with a velocity $v$ in free space and when it enters a medium, its velocity is reduced by $20%$ . The de Broglie wavelength of electron in the medium is $\alpha\lambda_{0}$ , where $\lambda_{0}$ is its de Broglie wavelength in free space. The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: The de Broglie wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by: $\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}$ Where h is Planck's constant. For a particle of constant mass (like an electron), the wavelength is inversely proportional to its velocity: $\lambda∝\frac{1}{v}$ Let the initial velocity in free space be $v_{0}$ . The velocity in the medium ( $v_{m}$ ) is reduced by $20%$ : $v_{m}=v_{0}-20%\text{of}v_{0}=v_{0}-0.20v_{0}=0.80v_{0}$ Let $\lambda_{0}$ be the wavelength in free space and $\lambda_{m}$ be the wavelength in the medium. $\frac{\lambda_{m}}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{v_{0}}{v_{m}}$ Substituting the value of $v_{m}$ : $\frac{\lambda_{m}}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{v_{0}}{0.80v_{0}}=\frac{1}{0.80}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\lambda_{m}}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{100}{80}=1.25$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=1.25\lambda_{0}=\alpha\lambda_{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha=1.25$ Therefore, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
The de Broglie wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by:

$\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}$

Where h is Planck's constant.

For a particle of constant mass (like an electron), the wavelength is inversely proportional to its velocity:

$\lambda∝\frac{1}{v}$

Let the initial velocity in free space be $v_{0}$ .

The velocity in the medium ( $v_{m}$ ) is reduced by $20%$ :

$v_{m}=v_{0}-20%\text{of}v_{0}=v_{0}-0.20v_{0}=0.80v_{0}$

Let $\lambda_{0}$ be the wavelength in free space and $\lambda_{m}$ be the wavelength in the medium.

$\frac{\lambda_{m}}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{v_{0}}{v_{m}}$

Substituting the value of $v_{m}$ :

$\frac{\lambda_{m}}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{v_{0}}{0.80v_{0}}=\frac{1}{0.80}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\lambda_{m}}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{100}{80}=1.25$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=1.25\lambda_{0}=\alpha\lambda_{0}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha=1.25$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

questions.explanation_html:
The Einstein's photoelectric equation states that the energy of incident photons to the work function of the metal and the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.

$K_{max}=h\nu-\Phi_{0}$

Where $K_{max}$ is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons, $h\nu$ is the energy of the incident photon (where h is Planck's constant and $\nu$ is frequency) and $\Phi_{0}$ is the work function of the metal, which is the minimum energy required to eject an electron.

The work function can also be expressed in terms of the threshold frequency $(v_{0})$ , which is the minimum frequency required for photoelectric emission:

$\Phi_{0}=hv_{0}$

The stopping potential ( $V_{0}$ ) is the negative potential applied to stop the most energetic photoelectrons. The work done by this potential equals the maximum kinetic energy:

$K_{max}=eV_{0}$

Substituting this into the photoelectric equation:

$eV_{0}=hv-\phi \Rightarrow V_{0}=(\frac{h}{e})v-\frac{\Phi_{0}}{e}$

The equation $V_{0}=(\frac{h}{e})v-\Phi_{0}$ is in the form of a straight line $(y=mx+c)$ .

The slope $m=\frac{h}{e}=$ constant for all metals, which is why the lines are parallel.

X -intercept represents the threshold frequency $(v_{0})$ , where $V_{0}=0$ . At this frequency, the incident energy exactly equals the work function $(\Phi_{0}=h\nu_{0})$ .

From the graph, we can identify the threshold frequencies for each metal:

For $X_{1}:v_{0} \approx 1.0 \times 10^{14}Hz$

For $X_{2}:v_{0} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{14}Hz$

For $X_{3}:v_{0} \approx 2.0 \times 10^{14}Hz$

We can see that $v_{01}<v_{02}<v_{03}$ . This means the work function of metal $X_{1}$ is the lowest $(\Phi_{1}<\Phi_{2}<\Phi_{3})$ .

Now, considering incident radiation of the same wavelength ( $\lambda$ ).

Since energy $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ , the incident energy is the same for all three metals.

Substituting this into the energy equation:

$K_{max}=E_{\text{incident}}-\Phi_{0}$

Since $E_{\text{incident}}$ is constant, the metal with the smallest work function ( $\Phi_{0}$ ) will result in the greatest kinetic energy ( $K_{\text{max}}$ ).

As metal $X_{1}$ has the lowest threshold frequency and thus the lowest work function, it will emit electrons with the greatest kinetic energy.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.question_text: The de Broglie wavelength of an oxygen molecule at $27^{\circ}C$ is $x \times 10^{-12}m$ . The value of $x$ is (take Planck's constant $=6.63 \times 10^{-34}J.s$ , Boltzmann constant $=1.38 \times 10^{-23}J/K$ , mass of oxygen molecule $=5.31 \times 10^{-26}kg$ )
questions.question_html: The de Broglie wavelength of an oxygen molecule at $27^{\circ}C$ is $x \times 10^{-12}m$ . The value of $x$ is (take Planck's constant $=6.63 \times 10^{-34}J.s$ , Boltzmann constant $=1.38 \times 10^{-23}J/K$ , mass of oxygen molecule $=5.31 \times 10^{-26}kg$ )
questions.explanation_text: For a gas molecule, the average kinetic energy $(K)$ is given by kinetic theory: $K=\frac{3}{2}k_{B}T$ where $k_{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant and T is the absolute temperature. The relationship between momentum ( p ) and kinetic energy ( K ) is: $p=\sqrt{2mK}$ Substituting K: $p=\sqrt{2m(\frac{3}{2}k_{B}T)}=\sqrt{3mk_{B}T}\dots(i)$ The de Broglie wavelength is defined as: $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}\dots$ From both the relations, $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{3mk_{B}T}}$ The given temperature is $27^{\circ}C$ . $T=27+273=300K$ The given mass is $5.31 \times 10^{-26}kg$ . So, the de Broglie wavelength is, $\lambda=\frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{3 \times 5.31 \times 10^{-26}}}=\frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{6595.02 \times 10^{-49}}}=\frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{6.595 \times 10^{-46}}}=\frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2.568 \times 10^{-23}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda \approx 2.58 \times 10^{-11}m=25.8 \times 10^{-12}m$ $\Rightarrow x \times 10^{-12}m=25.8 \times 10^{-12}m$ $\Rightarrow x \approx 26$ Therefore, the value of x is 26 . Hence, the correct option is (D).

$K=\frac{3}{2}k_{B}T$

where $k_{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant and T is the absolute temperature.

$p=\sqrt{2mK}$

Substituting K:

$p=\sqrt{2m(\frac{3}{2}k_{B}T)}=\sqrt{3mk_{B}T}\dots(i)$

The de Broglie wavelength is defined as:

$\lambda=\frac{h}{p}\dots$

From both the relations,

$\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{3mk_{B}T}}$

The given temperature is $27^{\circ}C$ .

$T=27+273=300K$

The given mass is $5.31 \times 10^{-26}kg$ .

So, the de Broglie wavelength is,

$\lambda=\frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{3 \times 5.31 \times 10^{-26}}}=\frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{6595.02 \times 10^{-49}}}=\frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{6.595 \times 10^{-46}}}=\frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2.568 \times 10^{-23}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda \approx 2.58 \times 10^{-11}m=25.8 \times 10^{-12}m$

$\Rightarrow x \times 10^{-12}m=25.8 \times 10^{-12}m$

$\Rightarrow x \approx 26$

Therefore, the value of x is 26 . Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: An electron of mass $m$ is moving in an electric field $\vec{E}=-2E_{o}\hat{i}(E_{o}=$ constant $>0)$ , with an initial velocity $\vec{V}=v_{o}\hat{i}(v_{o}=$ constant $>0)$ . If $\lambda_{o}=\frac{ℎ}{4mv_{o}}$ , its de Broglie wavelength at time $t$ is $____$ . ( $e=$ charge of electron)
questions.question_html:
An electron of mass $m$ is moving in an electric field $\vec{E}=-2E_{o}\hat{i}(E_{o}=$ constant $>0)$ , with an initial velocity $\vec{V}=v_{o}\hat{i}(v_{o}=$ constant $>0)$ . If $\lambda_{o}=\frac{ℎ}{4mv_{o}}$ , its de Broglie wavelength at time $t$ is

$____$ .

( $e=$ charge of electron)
questions.explanation_text: The force on an electron (charge -e) in an electric field $\vec{E}$ is $\vec{F}=-e\vec{E}$ . The electric field is given $\vec{E}=-2E_{0}\hat{i}$ , So, the force acting on electron is, $\vec{F}=(-e)(-2E_{0}\hat{i})=2eE_{0}\hat{i}$ Using Newton's second law of motion, $\vec{F}=ma\vec{a}$ the acceleration of electron is; $\vec{a}=\frac{\vec{F}}{m}=\frac{2eE_{0}}{m}\hat{i}$ Using the first equation of motion ( $\vec{v}=\vec{u}+\vec{a}t$ ), the final velocity of electron at any time $t$ is; $\vec{v}(t)=v_{0}+(\frac{2eE_{0}}{m})t$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{v}(t)=v_{0}(1+\frac{2eE_{0}t}{mv_{0}})$ The de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}=\frac{h}{mv}$ . Substituting the velocity: $\lambda_{t}=\frac{ℎ}{mv_{0}(1+\frac{2eE_{0}t}{mv_{0}})}$ It is given that $\lambda_{0}=\frac{h}{4mv_{0}} \Rightarrow \frac{h}{mv_{0}}=4\lambda_{0}$ . $\lambda_{t}=\frac{4\lambda_{0}}{1+\frac{2eE_{0}t}{mv_{0}}}$ Therefore, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
The force on an electron (charge -e) in an electric field $\vec{E}$ is $\vec{F}=-e\vec{E}$ .

The electric field is given $\vec{E}=-2E_{0}\hat{i}$ ,

So, the force acting on electron is,

$\vec{F}=(-e)(-2E_{0}\hat{i})=2eE_{0}\hat{i}$

Using Newton's second law of motion, $\vec{F}=ma\vec{a}$ the acceleration of electron is;

$\vec{a}=\frac{\vec{F}}{m}=\frac{2eE_{0}}{m}\hat{i}$

Using the first equation of motion ( $\vec{v}=\vec{u}+\vec{a}t$ ), the final velocity of electron at any time $t$ is;

$\vec{v}(t)=v_{0}+(\frac{2eE_{0}}{m})t$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{v}(t)=v_{0}(1+\frac{2eE_{0}t}{mv_{0}})$

The de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}=\frac{h}{mv}$ .

Substituting the velocity:

$\lambda_{t}=\frac{ℎ}{mv_{0}(1+\frac{2eE_{0}t}{mv_{0}})}$

It is given that $\lambda_{0}=\frac{h}{4mv_{0}} \Rightarrow \frac{h}{mv_{0}}=4\lambda_{0}$ .

$\lambda_{t}=\frac{4\lambda_{0}}{1+\frac{2eE_{0}t}{mv_{0}}}$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

questions.question_text: For a certain metal, when monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident, the stopping potential for photoelectrons is $3V_{0}$ . When the same metal is illuminated by light of wavelength $2\lambda$ , then the stopping potential becomes $V_{0}$ . The threshold wavelength for photoelectric emission for the given metal is $\alpha\lambda$ . The value of $\alpha$ is ______.
questions.question_html: For a certain metal, when monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident, the stopping potential for photoelectrons is $3V_{0}$ . When the same metal is illuminated by light of wavelength $2\lambda$ , then the stopping potential becomes $V_{0}$ . The threshold wavelength for photoelectric emission for the given metal is $\alpha\lambda$ . The value of $\alpha$ is ______.
questions.explanation_text: The energy of an incident photon is $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ , where $ℎ$ is the Planck’s constant, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $\lambda$ is the wavelength of incident light. According to Einstein’s equation of photoelectric effect; $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}=\phi+K_{max}$ Where $\phi$ is the work function is the minimum energy required to eject electron from the surface of metal, $(\phi=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}})$ and $K_{max}=eV_{s}$ ( $V_{s}$ is the stopping potential). So, $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}+eV_{s}$ Case 1: Wavelength is $\lambda$ , stopping potential is $3V_{0}$ . $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}+e(3V_{0})\dots(i)$ Case 2: Wavelength is $2\lambda$ , stopping potential is $V_{0}$ . $\frac{ℎc}{2\lambda}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}+eV_{0}$ $\Rightarrow 3(\frac{ℎc}{2\lambda})=3(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}})+3eV_{0}\dots(ii)$ On subtracting equation (i) from equation (ii): $(\frac{3ℎc}{2\lambda}-\frac{ℎc}{\lambda})=(\frac{3ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}-\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}})+(3eV_{0}-3eV_{0})$ $\frac{ℎc}{2\lambda}=\frac{2ℎc}{\lambda_{0}} \rightarrow \frac{1}{4\lambda}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}} \rightarrow \lambda_{0}=4\lambda$ $\Rightarrow \alpha\lambda=4\lambda \Rightarrow \alpha=4$ Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 4. Thus, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
The energy of an incident photon is $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ , where $ℎ$ is the Planck’s constant, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $\lambda$ is the wavelength of incident light.

According to Einstein’s equation of photoelectric effect;

$\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}=\phi+K_{max}$

Where $\phi$ is the work function is the minimum energy required to eject electron from the surface of metal, $(\phi=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}})$ and $K_{max}=eV_{s}$ ( $V_{s}$ is the stopping potential).

So, $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}+eV_{s}$

Case 1: Wavelength is $\lambda$ , stopping potential is $3V_{0}$ .

$\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}+e(3V_{0})\dots(i)$

Case 2: Wavelength is $2\lambda$ , stopping potential is $V_{0}$ .

$\frac{ℎc}{2\lambda}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}+eV_{0}$

$\Rightarrow 3(\frac{ℎc}{2\lambda})=3(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}})+3eV_{0}\dots(ii)$

On subtracting equation (i) from equation (ii):

$(\frac{3ℎc}{2\lambda}-\frac{ℎc}{\lambda})=(\frac{3ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}-\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}})+(3eV_{0}-3eV_{0})$

$\frac{ℎc}{2\lambda}=\frac{2ℎc}{\lambda_{0}} \rightarrow \frac{1}{4\lambda}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}} \rightarrow \lambda_{0}=4\lambda$

$\Rightarrow \alpha\lambda=4\lambda \Rightarrow \alpha=4$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 4. Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.explanation_text: To determine which color of visible light will cause the emission of photoelectrons from a metal with a work function of 3 eV, we need to consider the relationship between the photon energy, the work function, and the wavelength of light. The maximum kinetic energy ( $\text{KE}_{max}$ ) of the emitted photoelectrons is given by: $\text{KE}_{max}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi$ For photoemission to occur, the energy of the incident photons must be greater than the work function ( $\phi$ ): $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}>\phi$ This implies: $\lambda<\frac{ℎc}{\phi}$ Substitute the values $ℎ=4.135667696 \times 10^{-15}\text{eV} \cdot \text{s}$ , $c=3 \times 10^{8}\text{m/s}$ , and $\phi=3\text{eV}$ : $\lambda<\frac{1242}{3}\text{nm} \approx 414\text{nm}$ Since the wavelength must be less than 414 nm to cause emission, we need light with a shorter wavelength. Among the visible colors, blue light has a wavelength in this range, making it the correct choice. Thus, blue light will cause the emission of photoelectrons with this work function.
questions.explanation_html:
To determine which color of visible light will cause the emission of photoelectrons from a metal with a work function of 3 eV, we need to consider the relationship between the photon energy, the work function, and the wavelength of light.

The maximum kinetic energy ( $\text{KE}_{max}$ ) of the emitted photoelectrons is given by:

$\text{KE}_{max}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi$

For photoemission to occur, the energy of the incident photons must be greater than the work function ( $\phi$ ):

$\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}>\phi$

This implies:

$\lambda<\frac{ℎc}{\phi}$

Substitute the values $ℎ=4.135667696 \times 10^{-15}\text{eV} \cdot \text{s}$ , $c=3 \times 10^{8}\text{m/s}$ , and $\phi=3\text{eV}$ :

$\lambda<\frac{1242}{3}\text{nm} \approx 414\text{nm}$

Since the wavelength must be less than 414 nm to cause emission, we need light with a shorter wavelength. Among the visible colors, blue light has a wavelength in this range, making it the correct choice. Thus, blue light will cause the emission of photoelectrons with this work function.

questions.question_html: A proton of mass ' $m_{P}$ ' has same energy as that of a photon of wavelength ' $\lambda$ '. If the proton is moving at non-relativistic speed, then ratio of its de Broglie wavelength to the wavelength of photon is.
questions.explanation_text: To find the ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of a proton to the wavelength of a photon when they have the same energy, we follow these steps: Energy Equivalence : Both the proton and the photon have the same energy, denoted by E . Energy of the Photon : The energy of a photon with wavelength λ is given by: $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ Kinetic Energy of the Proton : Since the proton moves at a non-relativistic speed, its kinetic energy can be expressed as: $\text{KE}_{\text{proton}}=\frac{1}{2}m_{P}v^{2}=E$ Momentum of the Proton : The momentum p of the proton is derived from its kinetic energy: $p=\sqrt{2m_{P}E}$ de Broglie Wavelength of the Proton : The de Broglie wavelength λ_{proton} is: $\lambda_{\text{proton}}=\frac{ℎ}{p}=\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{2m_{P}E}}$ Ratio of Wavelengths : The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to the wavelength of the photon is: $\frac{\lambda_{\text{proton}}}{\lambda_{\text{photon}}}=(\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{2m_{P}E}}) \times (\frac{E}{ℎc})$ Simplifying, we get: $\frac{\lambda_{\text{proton}}}{\lambda_{\text{photon}}}=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{\frac{E}{2m_{P}}}$ Thus, the ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to the wavelength of the photon is $\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{\frac{E}{2m_{P}}}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To find the ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of a proton to the wavelength of a photon when they have the same energy, we follow these steps:

Energy Equivalence:

Both the proton and the photon have the same energy, denoted by E.

Energy of the Photon:

The energy of a photon with wavelength λ is given by:

$E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$

Kinetic Energy of the Proton:

Since the proton moves at a non-relativistic speed, its kinetic energy can be expressed as:

$\text{KE}_{\text{proton}}=\frac{1}{2}m_{P}v^{2}=E$

Momentum of the Proton:

The momentum p of the proton is derived from its kinetic energy:

$p=\sqrt{2m_{P}E}$

de Broglie Wavelength of the Proton:

The de Broglie wavelength λ_{proton} is:

$\lambda_{\text{proton}}=\frac{ℎ}{p}=\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{2m_{P}E}}$

Ratio of Wavelengths:

The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to the wavelength of the photon is:

$\frac{\lambda_{\text{proton}}}{\lambda_{\text{photon}}}=(\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{2m_{P}E}}) \times (\frac{E}{ℎc})$

Simplifying, we get:

$\frac{\lambda_{\text{proton}}}{\lambda_{\text{photon}}}=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{\frac{E}{2m_{P}}}$

Thus, the ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to the wavelength of the photon is $\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{\frac{E}{2m_{P}}}$ .

A photoemissive substance is illuminated with a radiation of wavelength $\lambda_{i}$ so that it releases electrons with de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda_{e}$ . The longest wavelength of radiation that can emit photoelectron is $\lambda_{o}$ . Expression for de-Broglie wavelength is given by:

questions.explanation_text: Kinetic Energy (K.E.): The kinetic energy of the emitted electron is given by subtracting the work function (W) of the material from the energy of the incident radiation (E). $\text{K.E.}=E-W$ Expressions for Energy: The energy of the incoming radiation $E$ is calculated using the formula: $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{i}}$ The work function $W$ , which is the minimum energy needed to release an electron, when the radiation wavelength is at its longest $\lambda_{0}$ , is: $W=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}$ De-Broglie Wavelength of the Electron: The de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda_{e}$ of the emitted electron is given by: $\lambda_{e}=\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{2m \cdot \text{K.E.}}}$ Substituting the Values: The kinetic energy of the emitted electron can be expressed in terms of energies as: $\frac{ℎ^{2}}{2m\lambda_{e}^{2}}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{i}}-\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}$ Final Expression for $\lambda_{e}$ : Solving for $\lambda_{e}$ , the de-Broglie wavelength of the electron, we have: $\lambda_{e}=\sqrt{\frac{ℎ}{2mc(\frac{1}{\lambda_{i}}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}})}}$ This expression determines the de-Broglie wavelength of the emitted electron based on the wavelengths of the incident and threshold radiation.
questions.explanation_html:
Kinetic Energy (K.E.): The kinetic energy of the emitted electron is given by subtracting the work function (W) of the material from the energy of the incident radiation (E).

$\text{K.E.}=E-W$

Expressions for Energy:

The energy of the incoming radiation $E$ is calculated using the formula:

$E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{i}}$

The work function $W$ , which is the minimum energy needed to release an electron, when the radiation wavelength is at its longest $\lambda_{0}$ , is:

$W=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}$

De-Broglie Wavelength of the Electron:

The de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda_{e}$ of the emitted electron is given by:

$\lambda_{e}=\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{2m \cdot \text{K.E.}}}$

Substituting the Values:

The kinetic energy of the emitted electron can be expressed in terms of energies as:

$\frac{ℎ^{2}}{2m\lambda_{e}^{2}}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{i}}-\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{0}}$

Final Expression for $\lambda_{e}$ :

Solving for $\lambda_{e}$ , the de-Broglie wavelength of the electron, we have:

$\lambda_{e}=\sqrt{\frac{ℎ}{2mc(\frac{1}{\lambda_{i}}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}})}}$

This expression determines the de-Broglie wavelength of the emitted electron based on the wavelengths of the incident and threshold radiation.

questions.question_text: A light source of wavelength $\lambda$ illuminates a metal surface and electrons are ejected with maximum kinetic energy of 2 eV . If the same surface is illuminated by a light source of wavelength $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ , then the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons will be (The work function of metal is 1 eV )
questions.question_html: A light source of wavelength $\lambda$ illuminates a metal surface and electrons are ejected with maximum kinetic energy of 2 eV . If the same surface is illuminated by a light source of wavelength $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ , then the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons will be (The work function of metal is 1 eV )
questions.explanation_text: Let's break down the problem step by step. The photoelectric equation is given by: $K_{\text{max}}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi$ where: $K_{\text{max}}$ is the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons. $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ is the energy of the incident photon. $\phi$ is the work function of the metal. For the initial light source of wavelength $\lambda$ , we know: $2\text{eV}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-1\text{eV}$ Solving for $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ gives: $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}=2\text{eV}+1\text{eV}=3\text{eV}$ Now, if the wavelength is halved to $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ , the photon energy becomes: $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda/2}=\frac{2ℎc}{\lambda}=2 \times 3\text{eV}=6\text{eV}$ The maximum kinetic energy for the new wavelength is then: $K_{\text{max}}^{'}=6\text{eV}-1\text{eV}=5\text{eV}$ Therefore, the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons when the surface is illuminated by a light source of wavelength $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ is 5 eV. The correct answer is Option A.
questions.explanation_html:
Let's break down the problem step by step.

The photoelectric equation is given by:

$K_{\text{max}}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi$

where:

$K_{\text{max}}$ is the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons.

$\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ is the energy of the incident photon.

$\phi$ is the work function of the metal.

For the initial light source of wavelength $\lambda$ , we know:

$2\text{eV}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-1\text{eV}$

Solving for $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ gives:

$\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}=2\text{eV}+1\text{eV}=3\text{eV}$

Now, if the wavelength is halved to $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ , the photon energy becomes:

$\frac{ℎc}{\lambda/2}=\frac{2ℎc}{\lambda}=2 \times 3\text{eV}=6\text{eV}$

The maximum kinetic energy for the new wavelength is then:

$K_{\text{max}}^{'}=6\text{eV}-1\text{eV}=5\text{eV}$

Therefore, the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons when the surface is illuminated by a light source of wavelength $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ is 5 eV.

The correct answer is Option A.

questions.question_html: An electron of mass ' m ' with an initial velocity $\vec{v}=v_{0}\hat{i}(v_{0}>0)$ enters an electric field $\vec{E}=-E_{o}\hat{k}$ . If the initial de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda_{0}$ , the value after time t would be
questions.explanation_text: Derivation of the de Broglie wavelength after time $t$ The de Broglie wavelength is given by $\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{p},$ where $ℎ$ is Planck's constant and $p$ is the momentum of the particle. Initial Conditions: Initially, the electron has a velocity $\vec{v}=v_{0}\hat{i},$ so its momentum is $p_{0}=mv_{0}.$ The initial de Broglie wavelength is therefore $\lambda_{0}=\frac{ℎ}{mv_{0}}.$ Effect of the Electric Field: The electron enters an electric field $\vec{E}=-E_{0}\hat{k}.$ For an electron with charge $-e$ , the force is given by $\vec{F}=-e\vec{E}=-e(-E_{0}\hat{k})=eE_{0}\hat{k}.$ This force causes an acceleration in the $\hat{k}$ direction: $a_{z}=\frac{F_{z}}{m}=\frac{eE_{0}}{m}.$ Momentum Components After Time $t$ : In the $\hat{i}$ direction, there is no force, so the momentum remains constant: $p_{x}=mv_{0}.$ In the $\hat{k}$ direction, starting from rest, the momentum becomes: $p_{z}=mv_{z}=m(a_{z}t)=eE_{0}t.$ Total Momentum of the Electron: The total momentum is the vector sum of the components: $p=\sqrt{p_{x}^{2}+p_{z}^{2}}=\sqrt{(mv_{0})^{2}+(eE_{0}t)^{2}}.$ New de Broglie Wavelength: Substituting the expression for the total momentum into the de Broglie relation gives: $\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{m^{2}v_{0}^{2}+e^{2}E_{0}^{2}t^{2}}}.$ Expressing this in terms of the initial de Broglie wavelength $\lambda_{0}=\frac{ℎ}{mv_{0}}$ : $\lambda=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{e^{2}E_{0}^{2}t^{2}}{m^{2}v_{0}^{2}}}}.$ This final expression matches the option: $\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{e^{2}E_{0}^{2}t^{2}}{m^{2}v_{0}^{2}}}}.$

The de Broglie wavelength is given by

$\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{p},$

where $ℎ$ is Planck's constant and $p$ is the momentum of the particle.

Initial Conditions:

Initially, the electron has a velocity

$\vec{v}=v_{0}\hat{i},$

so its momentum is

$p_{0}=mv_{0}.$

The initial de Broglie wavelength is therefore

$\lambda_{0}=\frac{ℎ}{mv_{0}}.$

Effect of the Electric Field:

The electron enters an electric field

$\vec{E}=-E_{0}\hat{k}.$

For an electron with charge $-e$ , the force is given by

$\vec{F}=-e\vec{E}=-e(-E_{0}\hat{k})=eE_{0}\hat{k}.$

This force causes an acceleration in the $\hat{k}$ direction:

$a_{z}=\frac{F_{z}}{m}=\frac{eE_{0}}{m}.$

Momentum Components After Time $t$ :

In the $\hat{i}$ direction, there is no force, so the momentum remains constant:

$p_{x}=mv_{0}.$

In the $\hat{k}$ direction, starting from rest, the momentum becomes:

$p_{z}=mv_{z}=m(a_{z}t)=eE_{0}t.$

Total Momentum of the Electron:

The total momentum is the vector sum of the components:

$p=\sqrt{p_{x}^{2}+p_{z}^{2}}=\sqrt{(mv_{0})^{2}+(eE_{0}t)^{2}}.$

New de Broglie Wavelength:

Substituting the expression for the total momentum into the de Broglie relation gives:

$\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{m^{2}v_{0}^{2}+e^{2}E_{0}^{2}t^{2}}}.$

Expressing this in terms of the initial de Broglie wavelength $\lambda_{0}=\frac{ℎ}{mv_{0}}$ :

$\lambda=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{e^{2}E_{0}^{2}t^{2}}{m^{2}v_{0}^{2}}}}.$

This final expression matches the option:

$\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{e^{2}E_{0}^{2}t^{2}}{m^{2}v_{0}^{2}}}}.$

questions.explanation_text: In the photoelectric effect, the stopping potential ( $V_{s}$ ) is determined by the equation: $V_{s}=\frac{ℎv-\phi}{e}$ where $ℎ$ is Planck's constant, $v$ is the frequency of the incident light, $\phi$ is the work function of the material, and $e$ is the charge of the electron. This shows that the stopping potential depends on the frequency of the incident light and the work function, not on the intensity of the light. The intensity of light ( $I$ ) affects the number of photons hitting the surface per second, given by: $I=\frac{\etaℎv}{A}$ where $\eta$ is the efficiency of photoelectron emission and $A$ is the area. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second ( $n$ ), which in turn increases the number of emitted electrons. However, the stopping potential remains unaffected by changes in intensity; it is solely influenced by the frequency of the incident light relative to the work function of the material.

questions.question_text:
A monochromatic light is incident on a metallic plate having work function $\phi$ . An electron, emitted normally to the plate from a point A with maximum kinetic energy, enters a constant magnetic field, perpendicular to the initial velocity of electron. The electron passes through a curve and hits back the plate at a point $B$ . The distance between $A$ and $B$ is :
(Given : The magnitude of charge of an electron is e and mass is $m,h$ is Planck's constant and c is velocity of light. Take the magnetic field exists throughout the path of electron)
questions.question_html: A monochromatic light is incident on a metallic plate having work function $\phi$ . An electron, emitted normally to the plate from a point A with maximum kinetic energy, enters a constant magnetic field, perpendicular to the initial velocity of electron. The electron passes through a curve and hits back the plate at a point $B$ . The distance between $A$ and $B$ is : (Given : The magnitude of charge of an electron is e and mass is $m,h$ is Planck's constant and c is velocity of light. Take the magnetic field exists throughout the path of electron)
questions.explanation_text: To determine the distance between points $A$ and $B$ (where the electron re-enters the metallic plate), we first need to understand the electron's behavior in a magnetic field. Maximum Kinetic Energy (KE) : The energy of the emitted electron can be given by the photoelectric equation: $\text{KE}_{max}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi$ Here, $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ is the energy of the incident photons, and $\phi$ is the work function of the metal. Momentum (p) : The momentum of the electron is related to its kinetic energy by the equation: $p=\sqrt{2m \cdot \text{KE}_{max}}=\sqrt{2m(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi)}$ Path of Electron in Magnetic Field : When an electron moves perpendicularly through a magnetic field, it follows a circular path. The radius $R$ of this path is given by: $R=\frac{p}{eB}$ where $e$ is the charge of the electron, and $B$ is the magnetic field strength. Distance Between $A$ and $B$ : Since the electron travels back to the plate, forming a complete semicircle, the distance between points $A$ and $B$ is twice the radius of this circular path: $d_{A-B}=2R=2(\frac{p}{eB})$ Substituting the expression for momentum, we find: $d_{A-B}=\frac{2\sqrt{2m(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi)}}{eB}=\frac{\sqrt{8m(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi)}}{eB}$ Therefore, the distance between $A$ and $B$ is $\frac{\sqrt{8m(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi)}}{eB}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the distance between points $A$ and $B$ (where the electron re-enters the metallic plate), we first need to understand the electron's behavior in a magnetic field.

Maximum Kinetic Energy (KE): The energy of the emitted electron can be given by the photoelectric equation:

$\text{KE}_{max}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi$

Here, $\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ is the energy of the incident photons, and $\phi$ is the work function of the metal.

Momentum (p): The momentum of the electron is related to its kinetic energy by the equation:

$p=\sqrt{2m \cdot \text{KE}_{max}}=\sqrt{2m(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi)}$

Path of Electron in Magnetic Field: When an electron moves perpendicularly through a magnetic field, it follows a circular path. The radius $R$ of this path is given by:

$R=\frac{p}{eB}$

where $e$ is the charge of the electron, and $B$ is the magnetic field strength.

Distance Between $A$ and $B$ : Since the electron travels back to the plate, forming a complete semicircle, the distance between points $A$ and $B$ is twice the radius of this circular path:

$d_{A-B}=2R=2(\frac{p}{eB})$

Substituting the expression for momentum, we find:

$d_{A-B}=\frac{2\sqrt{2m(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi)}}{eB}=\frac{\sqrt{8m(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi)}}{eB}$

Therefore, the distance between $A$ and $B$ is $\frac{\sqrt{8m(\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}-\phi)}}{eB}$ .

options.label: B

questions.explanation_text: Solution Explanation Among the four listed phenomena: Reflection of light Wave theory (Huygens’s principle, for example) adequately explains reflection. Refraction of light Wave theory also explains refraction via the change of wave speed in different media. Diffraction of light Wave theory (again, Huygens–Fresnel principle) explains the bending of waves around obstacles. Compton effect This involves inelastic scattering of photons by electrons (where the photon loses energy and is scattered with a longer wavelength). Wave theory alone cannot explain the discrete energy exchange and wavelength shift; it requires the particle (photon) concept from quantum theory. Hence, the phenomenon not explained by the (classical) wave theory is the Compton effect . Answer: (D) Compton effect.
questions.explanation_html:
Solution Explanation

Among the four listed phenomena:

Reflection of light

Wave theory (Huygens’s principle, for example) adequately explains reflection.

Refraction of light

Wave theory also explains refraction via the change of wave speed in different media.

Diffraction of light

Wave theory (again, Huygens–Fresnel principle) explains the bending of waves around obstacles.

Compton effect

This involves inelastic scattering of photons by electrons (where the photon loses energy and is scattered with a longer wavelength).

Wave theory alone cannot explain the discrete energy exchange and wavelength shift; it requires the particle (photon) concept from quantum theory.

Hence, the phenomenon not explained by the (classical) wave theory is the Compton effect.

Answer: (D) Compton effect.

questions.explanation_html:
Let's break down the problem step by step:

In the photoelectric effect, the energy of a photon is given by:

$ℎ\nu=\phi+K_{e}$

questions.question_text: Conductivity of a photodiode starts changing only if the wavelength of incident light is less than $660nm$ . The band gap of photodiode is found to be $(\frac{X}{8})eV$ . The value of $X$ is : (Given, $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34}Js,e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C$ )
questions.question_html:
Conductivity of a photodiode starts changing only if the wavelength of incident light is less than $660nm$ . The band gap of photodiode is found to be $(\frac{X}{8})eV$ . The value of $X$ is :

(Given, $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34}Js,e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C$ )
questions.explanation_text: To find the value of $X$ in the band gap $(\frac{X}{8})eV$ , we need to understand the relationship between the wavelength of light that can result in changes in the conductivity of a photodiode and the photodiode's band gap energy. The band gap energy ( $E_{g}$ ) of a material is the minimum energy required for an electron to transition from the valence band to the conduction band, thus creating a hole-electron pair and allowing conductivity to occur. When light with a certain wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) is incident upon the photodiode, if the energy of the photons is greater than or equal to the band gap energy of the photodiode, then the photons can excite electrons and change the conductivity of the photodiode. The energy of a photon ( $E_{pℎoton}$ ) is given by the equation: $E_{pℎoton}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ where: $ℎ$ is Planck's constant, which is given as $6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s. $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum ( $\approx 3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s). $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the incident light. Then the band gap energy in terms of electron volts is found by converting the energy from joules to electron volts (eV) using the charge of an electron $e$ ( $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C): $E_{g}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda e}$ Given that the photodiode starts conducting when the wavelength of light is less than $660nm$ , we should use this wavelength as the threshold wavelength $\lambda_{tℎresℎold}$ : $E_{g}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{tℎresℎold} \times e}$ $E_{g}=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}\text{J·s} \cdot 3 \times 10^{8}\text{m/s}}{660 \times 10^{-9}\text{m} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{C}}$ $E_{g}=\frac{6.6 \times 3 \times 10^{-26}}{660 \times 1.6}eV$ $E_{g}=\frac{19.8}{660 \times 1.6}eV$ $E_{g}=\frac{19.8}{1056}eV$ $E_{g}=\frac{18.75}{1000}eV$ $E_{g}=1.875eV$ Now, we have to compare this value to $(\frac{X}{8})eV$ to find the value of $X$ : $1.875=\frac{X}{8}$ $X=1.875 \times 8$ $X=15$ Therefore, the value of $X$ is 15. The correct answer is Option C.
questions.explanation_html:
To find the value of $X$ in the band gap $(\frac{X}{8})eV$ , we need to understand the relationship between the wavelength of light that can result in changes in the conductivity of a photodiode and the photodiode's band gap energy.

The band gap energy ( $E_{g}$ ) of a material is the minimum energy required for an electron to transition from the valence band to the conduction band, thus creating a hole-electron pair and allowing conductivity to occur. When light with a certain wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) is incident upon the photodiode, if the energy of the photons is greater than or equal to the band gap energy of the photodiode, then the photons can excite electrons and change the conductivity of the photodiode.

The energy of a photon ( $E_{pℎoton}$ ) is given by the equation:

$E_{pℎoton}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$

where:

  • $ℎ$ is Planck's constant, which is given as $6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s.
  • $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum ( $\approx 3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s).
  • $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the incident light.

Then the band gap energy in terms of electron volts is found by converting the energy from joules to electron volts (eV) using the charge of an electron $e$ ( $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C):

$E_{g}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda e}$

Given that the photodiode starts conducting when the wavelength of light is less than $660nm$ , we should use this wavelength as the threshold wavelength $\lambda_{tℎresℎold}$ :

$E_{g}=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda_{tℎresℎold} \times e}$

$E_{g}=\frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}\text{J·s} \cdot 3 \times 10^{8}\text{m/s}}{660 \times 10^{-9}\text{m} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{C}}$

$E_{g}=\frac{6.6 \times 3 \times 10^{-26}}{660 \times 1.6}eV$

$E_{g}=\frac{19.8}{660 \times 1.6}eV$

$E_{g}=\frac{19.8}{1056}eV$

$E_{g}=\frac{18.75}{1000}eV$

$E_{g}=1.875eV$

Now, we have to compare this value to $(\frac{X}{8})eV$ to find the value of $X$ :

$1.875=\frac{X}{8}$

$X=1.875 \times 8$

$X=15$

Therefore, the value of $X$ is 15. The correct answer is Option C.

questions.question_text: The de-Broglie wavelength of an electron is the same as that of a photon. If velocity of electron is $25%$ of the velocity of light, then the ratio of K.E. of electron and K.E. of photon will be:
questions.question_html: The de-Broglie wavelength of an electron is the same as that of a photon. If velocity of electron is $25%$ of the velocity of light, then the ratio of K.E. of electron and K.E. of photon will be:
questions.explanation_text: We know that the de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of a particle is given by: $\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{p}$ where: $ℎ$ is Planck's constant, $p$ is the momentum of the particle. For a photon (which has zero rest mass), its energy $E$ and momentum $p$ are related by the equation: $E=cp$ and its de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ is given by: $\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{E} \times \frac{1}{c}$ Now, since the photon and electron are said to have the same de-Broglie wavelength: $\lambda_{electron}=\lambda_{pℎoton}$ $\frac{ℎ}{p_{electron}}=\frac{ℎ}{E_{pℎoton}} \times \frac{1}{c}$ For the electron, its momentum $p_{electron}$ is given by: $p_{electron}=m_{e}v_{electron}$ where: $m_{e}$ is the electron's rest mass, $v_{electron}$ is the electron's velocity. The kinetic energy $K.E.$ of the electron is: $K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v_{electron}^{2}$ The question states that $v_{electron}$ is $25%$ ( $0.25c$ ) of the speed of light $c$ . So we write: $v_{electron}=0.25c$ Plugging this into the kinetic energy formula, we get: $K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}(0.25c)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e} \times \frac{1}{16}c^{2}$ $K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}$ For a photon, $p_{pℎoton}=\frac{E_{pℎoton}}{c}$ and hence its kinetic energy (which, for a photon, is simply its energy) is: $K.E._{pℎoton}=E_{pℎoton}=cp_{pℎoton}$ Now, comparing the kinetic energies: $\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}}{cp_{pℎoton}}$ Since $p_{electron}=p_{pℎoton}$ (from the de-Broglie relation), we can replace $p_{pℎoton}$ with $p_{electron}$ which is $m_{e}v_{electron}$ : $\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}}{m_{e}v_{electron}c}$ $\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}c}{0.25c}$ $\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{1}{32} \times \frac{1}{0.25}$ $\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{1}{32} \times 4$ $\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{1}{8}$ So the correct answer is Option C $\frac{1}{8}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
We know that the de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of a particle is given by:

$\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{p}$

where:

  • $ℎ$ is Planck's constant,
  • $p$ is the momentum of the particle.

For a photon (which has zero rest mass), its energy $E$ and momentum $p$ are related by the equation:

$E=cp$

and its de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ is given by:

$\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{E} \times \frac{1}{c}$

Now, since the photon and electron are said to have the same de-Broglie wavelength:

$\lambda_{electron}=\lambda_{pℎoton}$

$\frac{ℎ}{p_{electron}}=\frac{ℎ}{E_{pℎoton}} \times \frac{1}{c}$

For the electron, its momentum $p_{electron}$ is given by:

$p_{electron}=m_{e}v_{electron}$

where:

  • $m_{e}$ is the electron's rest mass,
  • $v_{electron}$ is the electron's velocity.

The kinetic energy $K.E.$ of the electron is:

$K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v_{electron}^{2}$

The question states that $v_{electron}$ is $25%$ ( $0.25c$ ) of the speed of light $c$ . So we write:

$v_{electron}=0.25c$

Plugging this into the kinetic energy formula, we get:

$K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}(0.25c)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e} \times \frac{1}{16}c^{2}$

$K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}$

For a photon, $p_{pℎoton}=\frac{E_{pℎoton}}{c}$ and hence its kinetic energy (which, for a photon, is simply its energy) is:

$K.E._{pℎoton}=E_{pℎoton}=cp_{pℎoton}$

Now, comparing the kinetic energies:

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}}{cp_{pℎoton}}$

Since $p_{electron}=p_{pℎoton}$ (from the de-Broglie relation), we can replace $p_{pℎoton}$ with $p_{electron}$ which is $m_{e}v_{electron}$ :

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}}{m_{e}v_{electron}c}$

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}c}{0.25c}$

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{1}{32} \times \frac{1}{0.25}$

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{1}{32} \times 4$

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{pℎoton}}=\frac{1}{8}$

So the correct answer is Option C $\frac{1}{8}$ .

questions.question_text: In Franck-Hertz experiment, the first dip in the current-voltage graph for hydrogen is observed at $10.2V$ . The wavelength of light emitted by hydrogen atom when excited to the first excitation level is ________ nm. (Given hc $=1245eVnm,e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C$ ).
questions.question_html: In Franck-Hertz experiment, the first dip in the current-voltage graph for hydrogen is observed at $10.2V$ . The wavelength of light emitted by hydrogen atom when excited to the first excitation level is ________ nm. (Given hc $=1245eVnm,e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}C$ ).
questions.explanation_text: The Franck-Hertz experiment provides evidence for quantized energy levels within atoms. When atoms are excited by electrons with a specific kinetic energy, they can jump to higher energy levels. Upon returning to lower levels, they emit photons whose energies correspond to the difference between these levels. The first dip in the current-voltage graph for hydrogen, observed at $10.2V$ , corresponds to the energy required to excite a hydrogen atom to its first excitation level. The wavelength of the light emitted when the atom returns to its ground state can be calculated using the energy of the photon emitted. To find the wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of light emitted, we use the relationship between energy ( $E$ ), Planck's constant ( $ℎ$ ), the speed of light ( $c$ ), and wavelength ( $\lambda$ ), given in the equation form as $E=\frac{ℎc}{\lambda}$ . However, we are given $ℎc$ in electron volts per nanometer ( $1245eV \cdot nm$ ), and the energy is also given in terms of voltage ( $10.2V$ ). First, we convert the energy into electron volts (eV) using the formula: $E=eV$ , where $e$ is the charge of an electron ( $1.6 \times 10^{-19}C$ ). The energy in electron volts can be directly calculated as: $E=10.2V \cdot 1.6 \times 10^{-19}C/electron=10.2eV$ , since $1V \cdot 1C=1eV$ by definition. Next, using the energy-wavelength relationship and the given value for $ℎc$ , the wavelength can be calculated as: $\lambda=\frac{ℎc}{E}$ Substituting the given values yields: $\lambda=\frac{1245eV \cdot nm}{10.2eV}$ This simplifies to: $\lambda=\frac{1245}{10.2}nm$ Calculating this gives: $\lambda \approx 122.06nm$ . Therefore, the wavelength of light emitted by the hydrogen atom when excited to the first excitation level is approximately $122.06nm$ .

questions.question_text: A proton, an electron and an alpha particle have the same energies. Their de-Broglie wavelengths will be compared as :
questions.question_html: A proton, an electron and an alpha particle have the same energies. Their de-Broglie wavelengths will be compared as :
questions.explanation_text: To determine the relationship between the de-Broglie wavelengths of a proton, an electron, and an alpha particle with the same energies, we need to use the de-Broglie wavelength formula: $\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{p}$ where $ℎ$ is Planck's constant and $p$ is the momentum of the particle. For particles with the same kinetic energy $E$ , we have: $E=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$ Solving for $p$ : $p=\sqrt{2mE}$ Substituting this into the de-Broglie equation, we get: $\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{2mE}}$ Since all three particles have the same energy $E$ , the de-Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass $m$ : $\lambda∝\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$ The masses of the particles are as follows: Mass of proton $m_{p}$ is approximately $1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg Mass of electron $m_{e}$ is approximately $9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg Mass of alpha particle $m_{\alpha}$ is approximately $4 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg (since it has 2 protons and 2 neutrons) Comparatively: Mass of alpha particle $m_{\alpha}$ is the largest. Mass of proton $m_{p}$ is intermediate. Mass of electron $m_{e}$ is the smallest. Therefore, the de-Broglie wavelength will be: Largest for the electron ( $\lambda_{e}$ ) Intermediate for the proton ( $\lambda_{p}$ ) Smallest for the alpha particle ( $\lambda_{\alpha}$ ) Hence, the correct order is: Option B: $\lambda_{\alpha}<\lambda_{p}<\lambda_{e}$
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the relationship between the de-Broglie wavelengths of a proton, an electron, and an alpha particle with the same energies, we need to use the de-Broglie wavelength formula:

$\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{p}$

where $ℎ$ is Planck's constant and $p$ is the momentum of the particle.

For particles with the same kinetic energy $E$ , we have:

$E=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$

Solving for $p$ :

$p=\sqrt{2mE}$

Substituting this into the de-Broglie equation, we get:

$\lambda=\frac{ℎ}{\sqrt{2mE}}$

Since all three particles have the same energy $E$ , the de-Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass $m$ :

$\lambda∝\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$

The masses of the particles are as follows:

  • Mass of proton $m_{p}$ is approximately $1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg
  • Mass of electron $m_{e}$ is approximately $9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg
  • Mass of alpha particle $m_{\alpha}$ is approximately $4 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg (since it has 2 protons and 2 neutrons)

Comparatively:

  • Mass of alpha particle $m_{\alpha}$ is the largest.
  • Mass of proton $m_{p}$ is intermediate.
  • Mass of electron $m_{e}$ is the smallest.

Therefore, the de-Broglie wavelength will be:

  • Largest for the electron ( $\lambda_{e}$ )
  • Intermediate for the proton ( $\lambda_{p}$ )
  • Smallest for the alpha particle ( $\lambda_{\alpha}$ )

Hence, the correct order is:

Option B:

$\lambda_{\alpha}<\lambda_{p}<\lambda_{e}$

questions.question_text: Which of the following phenomena does not explain by wave nature of light. A. reflection B. diffraction C. photoelectric effect D. interference E. polarization Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.question_html:
Which of the following phenomena does not explain by wave nature of light.

A. reflection

B. diffraction

C. photoelectric effect

D. interference

E. polarization

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

options.label: B
options.html: B, D only

options.label: C
options.html: A, C only

questions.explanation_text: The correct answer is Option A: C only. Reflection, diffraction, interference, and polarization are all phenomena that can be explained by the wave nature of light. These phenomena are evidence that light behaves as a wave, evident through various experimental observations: Reflection is the change in direction of a wavefront at an interface between two different media so that the wavefront returns into the medium from which it originated. The laws of reflection can be explained by treating light as waves. Diffraction is the bending of light around the corners of an obstacle or aperture into the region of geometrical shadow of the obstacle. This phenomenon is observed when a wave encounters an obstacle or a slit that is comparable in size to its wavelength, which is best explained by wave theory. Interference occurs when two or more waves superimpose to form a resultant wave of greater, lower, or the same amplitude. This phenomenon illustrates the wave nature of light through constructive and destructive interference patterns, such as those observed in the double-slit experiment. Polarization is a property applying to transverse waves that specifies the geometrical orientation of the oscillations. For light waves, this can be seen as the direction in which the electric field oscillates. Polarization can only occur with waves that have transverse components, further supporting the wave nature of light. On the other hand, the photoelectric effect cannot be explained solely by the wave nature of light. It is the emission of electrons or other free carriers when light shines on a material. Electrons emitted in this manner can be called photoelectrons. The phenomenon is best explained by Albert Einstein's quantum theory of light, where light is considered as quanta of energy called photons. This effect demonstrates the particle aspect of light, wherein each photon has a discrete packet of energy equal to $ℎf$ , where $ℎ$ is Planck's constant and $f$ is the frequency of the light. Thus, the photoelectric effect is the correct answer because it specifically requires the particle theory of light for its explanation, unlike reflection, diffraction, interference, and polarization, which are well-explained by the wave nature of light.
